Nos gusta la tecnología, el espacio y aprender cosas nuevas. Por eso nos gustó la idea de participar en el Space Apps Challenge y crear algo juntas. Nos encanta aportar ideas, buscar soluciones creativas y trabajar en equipo para llevarlas a la realidad. 

We love technology, space, and learning new things. That’s why we wanted to join the Space Apps Challenge and create something together. We enjoy sharing ideas, finding creative solutions, and working as a team to bring them to life.

summary:
The Forgotten Explorers is an interactive educational platform that brings new life to the stories of spacecrafts, rovers and equipment that NASA has left behind throughout its journey of space exploration. The aim is to explore the researched stories through various possible rounds of games, where school-aged students can discover why each object was launched, what it accomplished, the challenges it encountered, how its mission ended, and where it remains today. The platform combines an interactive exploration map, a digital archive, and engaging educational activities to transform scientific information into an accessible and immersive experience. 
Storytelling is the pillar behind the creation of the idea, through the stories created based on real experiences we aim to cultivate human curiosity, ingenuity, determination, and occasional failures behind some of NASA’s most remarkable achievements.
details:
“That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind”, across media that phrase has been cited, reused, shouted, and parodied since 1969. That one historic sentence was originally said by none other than Neil A. Armstrong, when he became the first man - along with LM pilot Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin, Jr. - to walk on the moon. Their story became history, it became a tale so well-known it reached classrooms all the way up to Uruguay, South America, where we heard and learned about their journey. Mankind reaching the moon is without a doubt the achievement of a century - a millennium even - but however remarkable that is, their journey did not start there. One single question sparked a challenge that will be strived to answer in this report: “what about the untold stories?”.

The project presented by us, the team Runaway Starlights (Estrellas Fugadas), is an interactive online web-based platform that aims to explore the untold stories of the moon landing. The project is born from the wish to spark curiosity and excitement in those who are just starting to harvest an interest in the vast space that surrounds us, which is why it is designed with school-aged children in mind.

Through an intuitive interface the player will be able to navigate the interactive website and go through the stages to reach the end. The journey begins on the first tab: Operations Center. After scrolling down, the game presents the user with two choices, either exploring Apollo’s traces in the moon or discovering how paths opened in Mars. Each path then presents the player (explorers) with a series of questions that divert into two possible options. For every step of the way there is a window narrating the story with the user as the main character; under it there is a special section showcasing the real facts extracted from NASA’s database center, so it’s just as educational as it is fun to play. By the end of the journey, the explorer’s achievements are stored in their personal archive, where they unlock their badge of recognition for completing their journey. Each accomplishment is met with a challenge they can achieve outside of the computer, related to the story they jus completed, so that the players can have hands-on experience reasoning like NASA’s experts. The website has a section called “My diary” where the explorers can scribble down thoughts, ideas and questions that have sparked during the game. Finally, on the tab “Activities” there are a few extra short games they can play, such as designing a rover, making decisions on difficult situations that may arise on a landing, and lastly, solving riddles. 

The objective behind the idea is simple: to inspire. We aim to cultivate the hunger of knowledge, the drive to think outside the box, and the will to dream beyond the stars. Unlike other online-based games, this does not end on the finish line, the purpose of the game is to get as many explorers as possible to engage in the contents of the real life events that led to the moon and Mars’s exploration, but also to ignite the fire to solve real issues that might arise when in the unknown. Such examples include observing and registering the phases of the Moon. Future challenges that will be added include figuring out a safe transportation for tree seeds all the way to space, to bring them back and study their growth compared to a control group of the same tree type that hadn’t been exposed to outer space. As a more developed version of the game will explore, this last example had been a real life problem that arose during an exploration; the containers had opened, almost losing the chance to study the effects of gravity in the trees’ early formation. (NASA, n.d.)

The demo presented for this year’s hackathon is an early version of the final product. For this stage’s creation the user interface was developed using Next.js and React to create a modern, responsive, and interactive web application. TypeScript was used to structure the code and improve its reliability, while CSS and Tailwind CSS were employed to design and customize the visual layout, ensuring a consistent and user-friendly experience across different devices. The interface incorporated Google Fonts, specifically DM Sans, DM Mono, and Playfair Display, to establish a distinctive visual identity and enhance readability. Development was carried out in Visual Studio Code, using Node.js and npm to manage dependencies and support the development process. NASA Science and NASA’s National Space Science Data Center (NSSDCA) serves as official scientific references, providing reliable information about space exploration and NASA missions. Finally, the website was deployed using Netify, making the interactive demo publicly accessible online.

Originality, interaction, collaboration and critical thinking were the pillars of this game’s foundation. As warned in the UNESCO paper “Guidance for Generative AI in Education and Research", the indiscriminate use of Generative AI can hinder people’s ability to articulate non-standardized answers and solutions (UNESCO, 2023). This is why out game is essential for the new generation of children growing up with AI intertwined into everyday life.

During the hackathon, what we aimed to achieve was the finished look of the demo and to present the video in time. However, when we first thought of the idea, we hoped to achieve much more with this project. What we wish for is to start implementing this in schools, so that we can strive for a better world, starting from the minds in the classroom.

The programming used for this project mainly consisted of TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, using Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS for web development. In regards to the accessibility of the interface, the demo is a web-based platform that can be accessed through a browser without requiring downloads or installations. Its design allows users to explore the content on different devices, including computers, tablets, and smartphones. The interfaces an intuitive, visually engaging, and easy to navigate game, particularly for elementary school children, encouraging independent exploration.

As we have stated before, the product presented is a demo, so numerous upgrades are in order. Firstly, our focus on the storytelling of the game will be on specific missions and pieces of equipment that NASA has done in the past. Furthermore, some of the future challenges the explorers will be faced with are as follows:

1- During the Apollo 13 (1970) mission an oxygen tank exploded. Engineers improvised an adapter to connect incompatible carbon dioxide filters. (NASA, 2009).

The challenge will read: “You have a square filter, but your spaceship only has a round opening. How would you connect them using the materials available on board?”

2-Apollo 11 (1969): Neil Armstrong manually guided the lunar module away from dangerous terrain while fuel was running low. (NASA, 2014).

The challenge will read: “Your spacecraft is approaching the Moon, but the landing area is covered in rocks. You have limited fuel. Where would you land?”.

3- Surveyor 3 (1967-1969): Apollo 12 astronauts recovered components from an abandoned lunar spacecraft for scientific analysis. (NASA, n.d.)

The challenge will read: “You discover an abandoned robot on the Moon. You can only bring one of its parts back to Earth. Which part would you choose, and what could scientists learn from it?”

Our project highlights educational, historical, and human perspectives on space exploration. We aim to inspire elementary school children to develop curiosity about the universe by introducing them to the people, challenges, and discoveries that shaped the history of space exploration. We also emphasize the importance of creativity, critical thinking, and independent problem-solving, encouraging children to ask their own questions and think beyond conventional boundaries rather than relying entirely on AI-generated answers. Ultimately, we want to show that space exploration does not start at rockets, but rather in curious minds.
